description:
Turritopsis dohrnii, the immortal jellyfish, can revert from a mature adult back into an immature polyp and start its life cycle over. It does this through transdifferentiation, where mature cells switch into entirely different cell types. Starvation, physical injury, or a sudden change in temperature or salinity can trigger it.

a biologist at Kyoto University, kept a colony of the jellyfish alive long enough to watch it rejuvenate itself 11 times over two years, the only person known to have managed it for any length of time.

In the wild, almost every individual is eaten or falls ill long before it ever needs to rejuvenate. Researchers are careful to call this biological immortality rather than invulnerability. Predation and disease still kill most of them outright.

The species has also quietly spread to every ocean on Earth, carried in the ballast water of cargo ships. A Smithsonian scientist called it a worldwide silent invasion. At about 4.5 millimetres across, it is easy to overlook.

In 2022, researchers compared its genome to a jellyfish that ages normally and found real differences in how it repairs DNA and renews stem cells, clues that could one day inform human ageing research.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turritopsis_dohrnii: covers the species' transdifferentiation process, reverting from a mature medusa back to the immature polyp stage, what triggers it (starvation, physical damage, sudden temperature or salinity change), Shin Kubota's captive colony at Kyoto University rejuvenating 11 times over two years, its worldwide spread via ballast water described by Smithsonian scientist Maria Miglietta as a silent invasion, and the explicit caveat that most individuals still die to predation or disease before ever needing to revert.
